planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Yulan magnolia opens its flowers very early, so avoid frost pockets and low-lying planting sites where cold air settles.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, organically rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Yulan magnolia has been cultivated in Chinese temple gardens for well over a thousand years and produces pure white, intensely fragrant, goblet-shaped flowers with nine thick tepals that open upright on bare branches in earliest spring before any leaves appear. It is one of the two parent species (with M. liliiflora) of the famous saucer magnolia (M. x soulangeana), and its influence shows in the substantial, waxy texture of its blooms. The rounded, spreading crown eventually reaches significant size, so give it a permanent, open site with room to develop. Water regularly during establishment and keep the root zone mulched; established trees tolerate short dry spells but perform best with consistent moisture.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade with shelter from strong wind; the very large leaves are prone to tearing in exposed sites, similar to bigleaf magnolia.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind that can shred the oversized leaves. Houpu magnolia is a large-leaved Chinese species that, unlike many magnolias, flowers after the leaves have emerged in late spring to early summer, producing huge, fragrant, creamy-white cup-shaped blooms up to 10 inches across surrounded by a whorl of large leaves. The thick, aromatic bark has been harvested for traditional Chinese medicine for over two thousand years, which has made wild populations rare; garden and arboretum specimens are propagated from cultivated stock rather than wild-collected material. Give it plenty of room and a deep, humus-rich soil, and expect a stately, coarse-textured specimen tree that takes center stage in a large landscape.

planting.note: Plant grafted, container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered, sunny site away from frost pockets; open flowers and buds are notably frost-tender, so avoid low ground and east-facing exposures where morning sun can hit frosted blooms.

directions: Plant grafted specimens in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered, sunny site protected from spring frost pockets. Campbell's magnolia is a native of the Himalayan foothills and one of the largest and most spectacular of all magnolia species, eventually forming a massive tree with huge, fragrant, pink to rose-purple saucer-shaped flowers up to 10 inches across that open on bare branches in late winter to early spring. Seed-grown trees can take two decades or more to reach flowering size, so named grafted clones are strongly preferred for the home garden, typically blooming within 10 years. Because the earliest flowers can be damaged by late frost, choose a sheltered site away from early morning sun and cold air drainage. Given the room to mature over many decades, it becomes one of the most magnificent flowering trees in cultivation.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Butterflies holds its rich yellow flower color best where spring nights stay cool, fading to a paler yellow in warmer climates.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Butterflies is a hybrid of Magnolia acuminata (cucumbertree) and M. denudata (Yulan magnolia) prized for its deep, non-fading yellow, tulip-shaped flowers with red stamens, which open on bare branches in mid-spring, somewhat later than star and saucer magnolias, reducing frost damage risk. It grows with a naturally compact, dense, pyramidal habit that fits smaller landscapes better than many yellow-flowered magnolia hybrids, and it begins flowering at a relatively young age. Site it where the spring bloom can be viewed against a dark background or evergreen backdrop for maximum contrast, and avoid hot, exposed western sites, since intense heat lightens the flower color.

common_name: Yellow Bird Magnolia (Upright Canary-Yellow Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Yellow Bird flowers emerge with the first leaves, which helps its late-spring blooms escape the frosts that damage earlier-blooming magnolias.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and introduced in 1981, Yellow Bird produces brilliant canary-yellow, goblet-shaped flowers roughly 3.5 inches across that open in mid to late spring as the foliage begins to unfurl, later than most other yellow magnolia hybrids, which helps protect the blooms from late frosts. It grows with a vigorous, upright, pyramidal habit that develops into a substantial specimen tree, making it a strong choice as a focal point or street tree where a true tree form is wanted rather than the shrubbier habit of many other yellow-flowered hybrids. Water deeply during the first two growing seasons to establish a strong root system, and mulch to keep roots cool.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Merrill is one of the most reliably floriferous and cold-hardy Loebner magnolia selections and begins flowering at a young age.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Raised at the Arnold Arboretum from seed sown in 1939 and named in 1952 for botanist Elmer Drew Merrill, this Loebner magnolia (a hybrid of M. kobus and M. stellata) is valued for its exceptionally profuse bloom of large, semi-double, white flowers lightly blushed with pink in early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows faster and more vigorously than many magnolias, quickly forming a rounded small tree, and flowers reliably at a young age even from modest-sized nursery stock. Merrill tolerates a wider range of soils, including clay, better than most magnolia species, and its later bloom time than star magnolia helps it dodge some late frosts. Prune only to remove dead, damaged, or crossing wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade; site Leonard Messel where its early-spring, frost-vulnerable flowers are sheltered from harsh wind and the most severe late frosts.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade. Raised at Nymans in Sussex, England, this Loebner magnolia (a hybrid of M. kobus and M. stellata) produces fragrant, star-shaped flowers with about twelve narrow tepals colored deep pink on the outside shading to white with a pink flush inside, opening on bare branches in early to mid spring. It forms a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed small tree and is widely regarded as one of the finest pink-flowered magnolias for small to medium gardens, combining good cold hardiness with a compact mature size. Water during establishment and dry spells, keep the root zone mulched, and avoid heavy pruning, since magnolias respond poorly to hard cuts.

common_name: Vulcan Magnolia (Deep Red New Zealand Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Vulcan flowers at a young age, often within a few years of planting.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Bred in New Zealand by noted magnolia hybridizer Felix Jury and introduced in 1989, Vulcan is renowned for some of the deepest flower color of any magnolia — large, goblet-shaped blooms up to 10 inches across in an intense deep wine-red to magenta that opens from equally dark buds on bare branches in late winter to early spring. It grows into a relatively compact, rounded small tree compared with many large-flowered hybrids, fitting more modest garden spaces, and it adapts to a wide range of soil types. The striking flower color and early, prolific bloom make it a dramatic specimen or focal-point planting; site it where the intense color can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Heaven Scent Magnolia (Fragrant Pink Upright Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade with shelter from cold winds.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from cold winds. Heaven Scent is a hybrid saucer-type magnolia noted for its intensely fragrant, cup-shaped flowers, pale pink shading to white with deeper rose-purple flushing toward the base of each tepal, opening in mid-spring on an upright, vigorous, conical tree. Its later bloom time compared with earlier saucer magnolia selections helps the flowers avoid some late-frost damage, and its strong, sweet fragrance carries well through the garden. It develops a more upright, tree-like form than many magnolia hybrids, making it useful where a narrower footprint is needed. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune only to remove damaged or crossing branches.

common_name: Black Tulip Magnolia (Deep Burgundy Compact Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Tulip blooms at a young age and is well suited to smaller residential landscapes.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Bred in New Zealand by Mark Jury as a cross between the deep red 'Vulcan' and the pink 'Iolanthe', Black Tulip carries some of the darkest flower color of any magnolia — thick-petaled, goblet-shaped blooms of deep burgundy-red that stay tightly cupped like a tulip rather than opening flat, giving the flowers an unusually rich, saturated look. It flowers over a long season, often reblooming sporadically after the main spring flush, and grows with a narrower, more upright habit than many magnolia hybrids, fitting tighter garden spaces well. Water deeply during establishment, mulch to conserve moisture, and avoid heavy pruning.

common_name: Diva Magnolia (Large-Flowered Deep Pink Sprenger's Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind and late frost pockets.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind. Diva is a selection of the Chinese species Magnolia sprengeri noted for exceptionally large, fragrant flowers, 6 to 8 inches across, with deep rose-pink to purple-pink outer tepals and paler, streaked interiors, opening on bare branches in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge. It grows into a substantial, broad-spreading tree over time, eventually becoming one of the most magnificent large pink-flowered magnolias in the garden, though it takes patience and space to reach full stature. Because the early flowers can be caught by late frost, choose a sheltered planting site away from cold air drainage, and water deeply during the first several growing seasons to establish a strong root system.
